title: Networking Foundations: Build, Address and Route
summary: Build real-looking networks in your browser: cable PCs, switches and routers, give them addresses, add static routes and prove it with ping. Then follow a DNS lookup from the root, write firewall rules for a school server and repair a broken office network. Split a switch into VLANs and hand out addresses with DHCP. Six labs with new numbers every time, and an optional path into Cisco Packet Tracer.
outcomes: Explain what PCs, switches and routers do and cable them correctly
Plan and set IPv4 addresses, masks and default gateways, including /30 router links
Configure router interfaces and static routes from forms or a Cisco-style command line
Test a network with ping, tracert and step-by-step packet simulation, there and back
Follow a DNS lookup through referrals and read A, NS, CNAME and MX records
Write least-privilege firewall rules and troubleshoot a network from the bottom up
Configure single-area OSPF with network statements, wildcards and passive interfaces, and show that it routes round a failed link
prerequisites: Comfort using a computer or phone browser. The Practical Tech Skills course (subnetting) helps but is not required.

lessons.title: Switches, routers and the cables between them
Check: devices and cables
lessons.intro: Four questions. Try again as often as you like.

questions.prompt: Which device joins two different IP networks?
questions.explanation: Routers forward packets between networks; switches join devices on the same network.

questions.prompt: What does a switch use to decide which port to send a frame out of?
options: The port number of the service
questions.explanation: Switches learn which MAC address is on which port.

questions.prompt: A new router interface has the right address but no traffic passes. What is the most likely cause?
options: It is still administratively down: it needs no shutdown
Routers need two cables per port
questions.explanation: Router interfaces stay shut down until turned on with no shutdown.

questions.prompt: What is a PC's default gateway?
options: The server it wants to reach
The router's address on the PC's own network
questions.explanation: The gateway is the router interface on the PC's network: the way out of it.

lessons.title: Addresses, masks and the default gateway
Lab: subnetting
lessons.intro: Work out where a network starts and ends, and whether two devices share it.

lessons.title: Check: addressing
lessons.intro: Four questions on masks and gateways.

questions.prompt: How many usable host addresses does a /30 network have?
questions.explanation: A /30 has 4 addresses; the network and broadcast addresses are not usable, leaving 2.

questions.prompt: Which address can be given to a PC on 192.168.10.0/24?
questions.explanation: .0 is the network address, .255 the broadcast, and 192.168.11.5 is on another network.

questions.prompt: A PC has 192.168.10.200 with mask 255.255.255.240 and gateway 192.168.10.1. Why can it not leave its network?
options: With that mask the gateway is on a different network from the PC
questions.explanation: A /28 around .200 covers .192–.207, so .1 is outside the PC's own network.

questions.prompt: A PC sends to an address on its own network. Where does the packet go?
options: Straight to the receiver, found with ARP
questions.explanation: Only traffic for other networks goes to the gateway.

lessons.title: Lab: build a routed network
lessons.intro: Start with an empty workspace. Place and cable the devices, address them from the plan, add a static route on each router and ping the server from every PC. Use Simulation if a ping fails.

questions.prompt: R1 and R2 share the link 172.16.0.0/30; R1 is .1 and R2 is .2. What next hop should R1 use for networks behind R2?
options: R2's address on the server's network
questions.explanation: The next hop is the other router's address on the network you share.

questions.prompt: A ping from a PC reaches the server, but the PC says Request timed out. What is the most likely cause?
options: The route back to the PC's network is missing
questions.explanation: The request arrived, so the way there works; the reply has no way back.

questions.prompt: Which route does a router use when several match?
options: The one with the longest prefix (most specific)
questions.explanation: Longest prefix match: the most specific route wins.

questions.prompt: What does the route ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 172.16.0.2 do?
options: Sends anything without a more specific route to 172.16.0.2
questions.explanation: It is a default route: used only when nothing more specific matches.

lessons.title: Lab: follow a DNS lookup
lessons.intro: You are the resolver. Start at the root, follow each referral, follow the CNAME, and find where the school's email goes.

questions.prompt: A server replies with NS records in the AUTHORITY section and no answer. What is it doing?
options: Referring you to servers closer to the name
Saying the name does not exist
questions.explanation: That is a referral: ask the servers it names next.

questions.prompt: Two MX records exist: 10 mail1 and 20 mail2. Which is tried first?
questions.explanation: The lowest preference number is tried first.

questions.prompt: The answer for portal.myschool is a CNAME. What next?
options: Look up the name the CNAME points to
Ask the root to delete it
questions.explanation: A CNAME is an alias: resolve the target name to get the address.

questions.prompt: Why do most lookups never reach a root server?
options: Root servers are switched off at night
Resolvers cache answers for their TTL
questions.explanation: Caching for the TTL means repeated lookups are answered from memory.

lessons.title: Firewalls: allow only what is needed
Lab: firewall rules for the school server
lessons.intro: Turn the policy into rules. Remember: the first match decides, and everything you do not allow is blocked.

lessons.title: Lab: repair the office network
lessons.intro: Three faults are hidden in a working-looking network. Test, find and fix them one at a time.

questions.prompt: A firewall has: 1 allow tcp any any, 2 allow tcp 192.168.20.0/24 port 22, then block everything. Who can use SSH?
questions.explanation: Rule 1 matches every TCP packet, so rule 2 never runs.

questions.prompt: Which source is right for a database that only the app server 10.1.1.20 may use?
questions.explanation: /32 means exactly one address: least privilege.

questions.prompt: Your PC says Destination host unreachable, from its own address. Where do you look first?
options: The PC's own settings and its gateway
questions.explanation: The PC could not reach its gateway: start with the PC, its cable and its settings.

questions.prompt: tracert shows the same two routers repeating until TTL expires. What is wrong?
options: A routing loop between those routers
questions.explanation: Packets going round between two routers is a routing loop.

questions.prompt: Why change one thing at a time while troubleshooting?
options: So you know which change fixed or broke something
questions.explanation: One change, one test: you learn what actually mattered.

lessons.title: VLANs, a router on a stick, and DHCP
Lab: VLANs, a router on a stick and DHCP
lessons.intro: The devices are placed and cabled. Put the staff and student ports in their VLANs, make the router port a trunk, add R1's subinterfaces, turn on DHCP on SRV1 with a relay for the students, set every PC to DHCP and ping the server. Use the forms or the command lines; check with show vlan brief and ipconfig.

lessons.title: Check: VLANs and DHCP
lessons.intro: Four questions on VLANs and DHCP.

questions.prompt: Which switch port carries several VLANs, each frame tagged with its VLAN number?
options: A port that is shut down
questions.explanation: Trunks carry many VLANs with 802.1Q tags; an access port carries one VLAN untagged.

questions.prompt: Two PCs on the same switch are in VLAN 10 and VLAN 20. What do they need to talk to each other?
options: A router (or a subinterface for each VLAN)
questions.explanation: Each VLAN is a separate network, so traffic between them must be routed.

questions.prompt: A student laptop shows 169.254.12.40 in ipconfig. What does it mean?
options: It got no answer from a DHCP server
questions.explanation: Windows uses a 169.254 address when DHCP fails.

questions.prompt: The DHCP server is in the staff VLAN. What lets students in another VLAN get addresses from it?
options: switchport mode access on the server's port
ip helper-address with the server's address on the students' router interface
A static route on the laptops
questions.explanation: The relay forwards the students' DHCP broadcast to the server, which uses the pool for their network.

lessons.title: OSPF: routers that learn the way

questions.prompt: What is the OSPF wildcard for a /30 router link (mask 255.255.255.252)?
questions.explanation: The wildcard is the mask turned inside out: 255.255.255.252 becomes 0.0.0.3.

questions.prompt: Why make a router's LAN port passive?
options: To stop the LAN's network being advertised
No router listens there, so hellos are pointless, but the network is still advertised
To turn the port off at night
questions.explanation: A passive interface sends no hellos but its network still goes into OSPF.

questions.prompt: Two routers on the same link do not become neighbours. Which of these could be the reason?
options: One router has a static default route
The PCs behind them use DHCP
questions.explanation: Neighbours must agree on the network, mask and area, and neither side may be passive.

questions.prompt: Three routers are joined in a triangle with OSPF. The link between R1 and R2 fails. What happens to traffic from R1 to R2's LAN?
options: It is lost until someone types a new route
It goes the long way round, through R3
It is sent back to the PC
OSPF shuts down the whole network
questions.explanation: OSPF notices the failed link and works out the next best path, through R3.

lessons.title: Optional: build the routed network in Packet Tracer
lessons.body:
Build the network from the *Build a routed network* lab in Cisco Packet Tracer: two PCs on a switch, two routers joined by a /30 link, and a server. Use the same kind of addressing plan, add static routes both ways, and check that every PC can ping the server.

Save your work and hand in the **.pkt** file, with two or three sentences on anything that behaved differently from the network builder.
